Last night I got my SA56004ED temperature sensor communicating over I2C on an Arduino. I was disappointed to find that the Arduino can only read 32 bytes of data from one device address. This is a problem for this chip because the temperature is broken up into two bytes: local temperature high byte at 0x00 and local temperature low byte at 0x22 (which is 34 in decimal and just outside the 32 byte limit). Although the low byte only holds the decimal places of the temperature, this is important when you're measuring Celsius because there's a decent jump in temperature between each whole number.

Since this chip also has the capability of measuring remote temperature using an external diode (and both the high and low bytes are in the 32 byte range), I will hook that circuit up tonight and see how well it works. I wish I didn't have to do it that way because it adds components to an otherwise simple circuit, and my "remote" circuitry is going to be placed right beside the local chip. Now I can see why I couldn't find any existing tutorials for using this chip with an Arduino, but this was the only temperature sensor I could find in my parts.

object.content: That's an interesting limitation on the Arduino that I didn't realize. What's the advantage of a chip like this over a thermistor?

I like the DS18b20, it was super easy to use with the Arduino:
http://contractorwolf.wordpress.com/arduino-temperature-probe/

The only advantage is that I didn't have to order this. This was the only digital temperature sensor I had that I could find and I actually removed it from an unused dev board. 
But now that I think about it I might have a thermistor someone. I didn't think of looking for an "analog" sensor. I'll look around for it tonight and see what I can find.

object.content:
+Dillon Nichols 
Having not played with I2C on an Arduino yet, I assumed the sw supported not only device address, but also sub addresses to get access to the device registers.
Can anyone shed some light on this matter ?

I think I figured out how to request data from a specific register. The code is below. The Wire.send() line asks for the register to be sent next, so I should be able to change it to Wire.send(0x22); and get the lower temperature byte.  This function isn't listed in the library documentation for the Wire library on the Arduino page so that's how I missed it. And it doesn't have a very good name for what it does. Hopefully it isn't listed because it was depreciated. 

Wire.beginTransmission(temp_address); //Start talking
  Wire.send(0); //Ask for Register zero
  Wire.endTransmission(); //Complete Transmission
  Wire.requestFrom(temp_address, 1); //Request 1 Byte
  while(Wire.available() == 0); //wait for response
  int c = Wire.receive(); // Get the temp
